units.title: Numbers on a Computer
units.blurb: See how a computer stores numbers, where errors come from, and how to tell a hard problem from a bad method.

units.title: Solving Equations
units.blurb: Find roots with bisection, fixed-point iteration, Newton's method and the secant method, and measure how fast each one converges.

units.title: Linear Systems on a Computer
units.blurb: Solve Ax = b reliably: the cost of elimination, pivoting, LU, norms and condition numbers, and iterative methods.

units.title: Interpolation
units.blurb: Pass polynomials and splines through data points, and see when adding points helps and when it hurts.

units.title: Derivatives and Integrals
units.blurb: Approximate derivatives and integrals, choose step sizes, and squeeze out extra accuracy with extrapolation and smart nodes.

units.title: Differential Equations
units.blurb: Measure the error of ODE solvers, solve systems, keep steps stable, and turn boundary value problems and the heat equation into linear algebra.

units.title: Least Squares and Eigenvalues
units.blurb: Fit data stably with QR, and find eigenvalues by iteration.

topics.title: Absolute and Relative Error
topics.short: Absolute error is |approximation − true value|; relative error divides by |true value| and tells how many significant digits are correct.
topics.trouble: Students divide by the approximation instead of the true value, or compare absolute errors of numbers of very different sizes.

topics.title: Binary Fractions
topics.short: Convert a decimal fraction to base 2 by doubling and keeping the whole-number parts: 0.1 becomes 0.000110011… and never ends.
topics.trouble: Students expect every short decimal to have a short binary form. Only fractions whose denominator in lowest terms is a power of 2 end in binary.

topics.title: Floating-Point Numbers
topics.short: A float stores ±1.f × 2ᵉ with a fixed number of bits, so the gaps between floats grow with their size; machine epsilon, 2⁻⁵² ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ in double precision, sets the relative precision.
topics.trouble: Students expect 0.1 + 0.2 to equal 0.3 exactly on a computer, or picture floating-point numbers as evenly spaced.

topics.title: Round-Off and Cancellation
topics.short: Subtracting nearly equal numbers wipes out correct digits; rewrite the formula to avoid it, as in √(x + 1) − √x = 1/(√(x + 1) + √x).
topics.trouble: Students trust every digit a computer prints. After cancellation the leading digits are gone, and most of the digits left are round-off.

topics.title: Truncation Error and Order of Accuracy
topics.short: Stopping an infinite process, such as a Taylor series or a limit, leaves truncation error; an error of order hᵖ shrinks by a factor of about 2ᵖ when h is halved.
topics.trouble: Students mix up truncation error, which comes from the method, with round-off error, which comes from storing a limited number of digits.

topics.title: Conditioning of a Problem
topics.short: The condition number κ = |x f′(x)/f(x)| says how much a relative change in the input is magnified in the output, whatever method is used.
topics.trouble: Students blame the method when the problem itself is ill-conditioned. No method can give f(x) to more correct digits than the input allows.

topics.title: Stable and Unstable Algorithms
topics.short: A stable algorithm gives the exact answer to a slightly changed problem, so two formulas for the same quantity can behave very differently in floating point.
topics.trouble: Students think a stable algorithm always gives an accurate answer. On an ill-conditioned problem, even a stable method can be far off; stability and accuracy are different things.

topics.title: Horner's Method
topics.short: Evaluate a polynomial by nesting, ((aₙx + aₙ₋₁)x + ⋯)x + a₀, with only n multiplications and n additions.
topics.trouble: Students start nesting from the constant term instead of the leading coefficient, or skip a missing power instead of writing a 0 coefficient for it.

topics.title: The Bisection Method
topics.short: Keep halving an interval where f changes sign; after n steps the midpoint is within (b − a)/2ⁿ⁺¹ of a root.
topics.trouble: Students start without checking for a sign change, or use a function with a break: tan x changes sign on [1, 2] at an asymptote, not at a root.

topics.title: Fixed-Point Iteration
topics.short: Rewrite f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and repeat xₙ₊₁ = g(xₙ); it converges near the fixed point when |g′| < 1 there.
topics.trouble: Students expect every rearrangement to work. To solve x² = 2, x = 2/x bounces between two values forever, while x = (x + 2/x)/2 converges fast.

topics.title: Order of Convergence
topics.short: If eₙ₊₁ ≈ C eₙᵖ, the method has order p: a linear method gains about the same number of digits each step, and a quadratic one doubles them.
topics.trouble: Students estimate the order from the ratio eₙ₊₁/eₙ. The order comes from logarithms: p ≈ ln(eₙ₊₁/eₙ) / ln(eₙ/eₙ₋₁).

topics.title: Newton's Method: Speed and Failure
topics.short: Near a simple root, Newton's method converges quadratically; a poor start, a tangent that is nearly flat, or a multiple root can make it fail or slow down.
topics.trouble: Students assume Newton's method always converges. For f(x) = x³ − 2x + 2 starting at 0, it cycles between 0 and 1 forever.

topics.title: The Secant Method
topics.short: Replace f′ with the slope through the last two points; it needs no derivative, and its order is about 1.618.
topics.trouble: Students keep a pair that brackets the root, as in bisection. The secant method always uses the two most recent points, which need not bracket it.

topics.title: Newton's Method for Systems
topics.short: Solve J(x) Δ = −F(x) with the Jacobian matrix J, then update x to x + Δ.
topics.trouble: Students put the partial derivatives in the wrong places (row i holds the partials of Fᵢ), or forget the minus sign on F(x).

topics.title: The Cost of Elimination
topics.short: Gaussian elimination takes about 2n³/3 arithmetic operations and each triangular solve about n², so doubling n multiplies the work by about 8.
topics.trouble: Students compute A⁻¹ to solve Ax = b. Elimination is cheaper and usually more accurate.

topics.title: Partial Pivoting
topics.short: Before each elimination step, swap up the row whose entry in the pivot column is largest in size, so tiny pivots do not magnify round-off.
topics.trouble: Students swap rows only when a pivot is exactly 0, but in floating point a tiny pivot such as 10⁻²⁰ does just as much damage.

topics.title: Solving with PA = LU
topics.short: Factor once with pivoting, then solve Ly = Pb by forward substitution and Ux = y by back substitution for each new right-hand side b.
topics.trouble: Students forget to apply the row swaps P to b before forward substitution.

topics.title: Vector and Matrix Norms
topics.short: Measure size with ‖x‖₁, ‖x‖₂ and ‖x‖∞; the matching matrix norms ‖A‖₁ and ‖A‖∞ are the largest absolute column sum and the largest absolute row sum.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the two: ‖A‖∞ uses rows, ‖A‖₁ uses columns, and both add absolute values.

topics.title: The Condition Number of a Matrix
topics.short: κ(A) = ‖A‖ ‖A⁻¹‖ bounds how much a relative change in b can grow in x; a small residual does not guarantee a small error.
topics.trouble: Students trust a solution because its residual b − Ax is tiny. When the matrix is ill-conditioned, the error in x can still be large.

topics.title: Jacobi Iteration
topics.short: Solve each equation for its own variable and update every variable at once from the previous values; strict diagonal dominance guarantees convergence.
topics.trouble: Students run the iteration on the equations as given, even when listing them in another order would make the system diagonally dominant; in the wrong order the iteration can diverge.

topics.title: Gauss–Seidel Iteration
topics.short: Use each new value as soon as it is computed; for strictly diagonally dominant systems it converges, usually faster than Jacobi.
topics.trouble: Students keep using last sweep's values for variables already updated in this sweep, which is Jacobi's method, not Gauss–Seidel.

topics.title: Lagrange Interpolation
topics.short: Exactly one polynomial of degree at most n passes through n + 1 points with different x-values; build it from basis polynomials that are 1 at one node and 0 at the others.
topics.trouble: Students expect degree n + 1 for n + 1 points, or build a basis polynomial that is 0 at the wrong nodes.

topics.title: Newton's Divided Differences
topics.short: Build the interpolating polynomial one point at a time from a table of divided differences, without starting over.
topics.trouble: Students divide by the gap between neighboring x-values at every level, instead of the gap between the x-values at the two ends of the entry's span.

topics.title: Interpolation Error
topics.short: f(x) − p(x) = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n + 1)! · (x − x₀)(x − x₁)⋯(x − xₙ) for some ξ in the interval.
topics.trouble: Students use the nth derivative instead of the (n + 1)st, or forget the product of (x − xᵢ), which is largest near the ends of the interval.

topics.title: Runge's Phenomenon and Chebyshev Nodes
topics.short: High-degree interpolation at equally spaced points can swing wildly near the ends; Chebyshev nodes, bunched toward the ends, fix it.
topics.trouble: Students expect more equally spaced points always to give a better fit. For 1/(1 + 25x²) on [−1, 1], the error grows as the degree goes up.

topics.title: Cubic Splines
topics.short: Join cubic pieces that match values, slopes and second derivatives at the knots; a natural spline has second derivative 0 at both ends.
topics.trouble: Students match only values and slopes, which leaves the curvature jumping at the knots, or forget the two end conditions.

topics.title: Finite-Difference Derivatives
topics.short: The forward difference (f(x + h) − f(x))/h has error of order h; the central difference (f(x + h) − f(x − h))/(2h) has error of order h².
topics.trouble: Students divide the central difference by h instead of 2h.

topics.title: The Best Step Size
topics.short: Shrinking h cuts truncation error but magnifies round-off, so the total error is smallest at a moderate h, about 10⁻⁸ for a forward difference in double precision.
topics.trouble: Students make h as small as possible. Below the best h, round-off error grows like ε/h and swamps the answer.

topics.title: Richardson Extrapolation
topics.short: Combine results at h and h/2 to cancel the leading error term: for a method with error of order h², use (4A(h/2) − A(h))/3.
topics.trouble: Students use the weights for the wrong order. (4A(h/2) − A(h))/3 cancels an h² term; 2A(h/2) − A(h) cancels an h term.

topics.title: Error in the Trapezoid and Simpson's Rules
topics.short: The composite trapezoid rule has error of order h² and Simpson's rule of order h⁴, so halving h cuts the error by about 4 or 16.
topics.trouble: Students think Simpson's rule is exact only for quadratics. It is exact for cubics too.

topics.title: Romberg Integration
topics.short: Apply Richardson extrapolation to trapezoid estimates again and again to fill a triangle of better and better values.
topics.trouble: Students use the factor 4 in every column. Column m uses (4ᵐ · finer − coarser)/(4ᵐ − 1).

topics.title: Gaussian Quadrature
topics.short: Choose the nodes as well as the weights: two points at ±1/√3 integrate every cubic exactly on [−1, 1].
topics.trouble: Students move the nodes to [a, b] but forget to multiply by (b − a)/2.

topics.title: Adaptive Integration
topics.short: Compare Simpson's rule on an interval with Simpson's rule on its two halves; the difference divided by 15 estimates the error, and only the intervals that fail the test are split.
topics.trouble: Students split every interval when only the ones that fail the error test need it.

topics.title: Local and Global Error
topics.short: Each Euler step makes a local error of order h², and the 1/h steps together leave a global error of order h.
topics.trouble: Students expect the error at the end to be the size of one step's error. The errors of all the steps add up, which costs one power of h.

topics.title: Systems and Higher-Order Equations
topics.short: Rewrite y″ = f(t, y, y′) as a first-order system, then take Euler or Runge–Kutta steps with vectors.
topics.trouble: Students forget that each component needs its own starting value: a second-order equation needs both y(0) and y′(0).

topics.title: Stability of Euler's Method
topics.short: For y′ = λy with λ < 0, Euler's method gives yₙ = (1 + hλ)ⁿ y₀, which stays bounded only when |1 + hλ| ≤ 1, that is, when h ≤ 2/|λ|.
topics.trouble: Students think a method with small truncation error works with any step size. When h is too large for the problem, the steps blow up even though the true solution decays.

topics.title: Backward Euler and Stiff Equations
topics.short: Backward Euler uses the slope at the new point, so each step means solving for yₙ₊₁; for y′ = λy with λ < 0 it is stable for every step size.
topics.trouble: Students take the backward Euler step with the slope at the old point, which is forward Euler again.

topics.title: Multistep Methods
topics.short: Adams–Bashforth methods reuse earlier slopes, as in yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + (h/2)(3fₙ − fₙ₋₁), and need a one-step method to get started.
topics.trouble: Students try to take the first step with the two-step formula before there is an earlier slope to use.

topics.title: Boundary Value Problems by Finite Differences
topics.short: Replace y″ by (yᵢ₊₁ − 2yᵢ + yᵢ₋₁)/h² at each inside grid point to get a tridiagonal linear system.
topics.trouble: Students treat the known boundary values as unknowns, or forget to move them to the right-hand side.

topics.title: The Heat Equation: An Explicit Scheme
topics.short: uᵢⁿ⁺¹ = uᵢⁿ + r(uᵢ₊₁ⁿ − 2uᵢⁿ + uᵢ₋₁ⁿ) with r = kΔt/Δx² is stable only when r ≤ 1/2.
topics.trouble: Students refine the space grid without shrinking the time step. Halving Δx means cutting Δt by a factor of 4 to keep r ≤ 1/2.

topics.title: Least Squares with QR
topics.short: Solve Rx = Qᵀb instead of the normal equations, because forming AᵀA squares the condition number.
topics.trouble: Students form AᵀA for every least-squares problem. Since κ(AᵀA) = κ(A)², digits are lost when A is ill-conditioned.

topics.title: The Power Method
topics.short: Multiply by A and rescale, again and again; the vector turns toward the dominant eigenvector at a rate set by |λ₂/λ₁|.
topics.trouble: Students expect convergence when the two largest eigenvalues have the same size, such as 2 and −2. Then the iterates never settle.

topics.title: Inverse and Shifted Power Methods
topics.short: Run the power method on (A − sI)⁻¹, solving a system each step instead of inverting, to find the eigenvalue of A closest to the shift s.
topics.trouble: Students report the eigenvalue μ of (A − sI)⁻¹ as the answer. The eigenvalue of A is s + 1/μ.

topics.title: Gershgorin Disks
topics.short: Every eigenvalue lies in a disk centered at a diagonal entry aᵢᵢ, with radius equal to the sum of the other |aᵢⱼ| in that row.
topics.trouble: Students include |aᵢᵢ| in the radius, or expect each disk to hold exactly one eigenvalue; when disks overlap, one of them can hold none.

topics.title: The QR Algorithm
topics.short: Factor Aₖ = QₖRₖ and set Aₖ₊₁ = RₖQₖ; each new matrix is similar to A, and its diagonal approaches the eigenvalues.
topics.trouble: Students multiply the factors back in the same order, QₖRₖ, which just gives Aₖ again.
